dataset.what_one_row_represents: eurovision.csv: one act in one round of one year (final, grand-final, or semi-final). eurovision-votes.csv: one country-to-country point allocation in one round of one year, separated by jury vs televote.
dataset.geographic_scope: European Broadcasting Union countries plus Australia and Israel; 52 distinct competing countries

ana_01.label: Ireland and Sweden tie for most wins (7 each)
ana_01.content: Across all 66 contests held between 1956 and 2022, Ireland has won seven times and Sweden six. (The dataset stops at 2022; Sweden tied Ireland's record in 2023.) The Netherlands, France and Luxembourg all sit at 5; the United Kingdom also has 5; Israel has 4. Together, only 27 of the 52 competing countries have ever won. Ireland's wins are concentrated in an unmatched run: 1992 (Linda Martin), 1993 (Niamh Kavanagh), 1994 (Paul Harrington and Charlie McGettigan) - the only three-in-a-row in contest history - plus 1996 (Eimear Quinn), 1980 and 1987 (Johnny Logan), and 1970 (Dana).

calculation.output: Ireland 7, Sweden 6, Netherlands 5, France 5, Luxembourg 5, United Kingdom 5, Israel 4, Ukraine 3, Italy 3, Denmark 3, Norway 3, Switzerland 2, Spain 2, Germany 2, Austria 2, Serbia 1, Greece 1, Turkey 1, Latvia 1, Estonia 1, Russia 1, Yugoslavia 1, Azerbaijan 1, Belgium 1, Portugal 1, Monaco 1, Finland 1; countries with at least one win: 27

data_table.description: Eurovision wins by country, all-time through 2022.

notable_instance.name: ABBA - Waterloo (Sweden 1974)
notable_instance.value: Sweden's first of 6 wins; voted contest's all-time best song in 2005

ana_02.label: Cyprus and Greece: the most extreme bilateral 12-point pair
ana_02.content: In 35 grand finals where both countries competed and were eligible to vote for each other, Cyprus has awarded Greece 12 points 28 times - 80% of all opportunities. Greece has awarded Cyprus 12 points 22 times in 31 opportunities (71%). No other directed pair in the data comes close: the next-best is Belarus to Russia at 67% (12 of 18). The chance of awarding any specific country 12 points by random chance in a 26-country final is about 1 in 25, or 4%. Cyprus's 80% rate is therefore roughly 20 times the chance baseline.

calculation.output:
Cyprus -> Greece: 28 twelves in 35 opportunities (80.0%), 394 total points
Greece -> Cyprus: 22 twelves in 31 opportunities (71.0%), 331 total points
Montenegro -> Serbia: 11 twelves in 12 (91.7%) [smaller sample]
Belarus -> Russia: 12 in 18 (66.7%)
Moldova -> Romania: 11 in 15 (73.3%)
Romania -> Moldova: 11 in 16 (68.8%)

data_table.description: Top directed pairs by 12-point gifting rate, in finals only, minimum 5 opportunities.

ana_03.label: Reciprocal 12-point exchanges - mutual gifting
ana_03.content: Cyprus and Greece exchange 12 points more than any other pair in the dataset: Cyprus has given Greece 28 maximum scores and Greece has given Cyprus 22, for a combined 50 mutual 12-point exchanges. The next-closest pairs are far behind: Moldova-Romania at 22, Denmark-Sweden at 17, Norway-Sweden at 17, Portugal-Spain at 13. Eight of the top 12 reciprocal pairs lie within the same broad regional bloc (Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, ex-Soviet, Iberian, or Greek-Cypriot).

calculation.output:
Cyprus<->Greece total mutual 12s: 50 (28 + 22)
Moldova<->Romania: 22 (11 + 11)
Denmark<->Sweden: 17 (13 + 4)
Norway<->Sweden: 17 (10 + 7)
Portugal<->Spain: 13
Ireland<->Sweden: 12
Armenia<->Russia: 12 (7+5)
Denmark<->Iceland: 12 (4+8)

data_table.description: Top reciprocal 12-point pairs (sum of mutual 12-point allocations).

ana_04.label: Inside the bloc, the average vote is 2.3x higher
ana_04.content: Across all final-round country-to-country votes since 1975, when both voter and recipient sit in the same regional bloc (Nordic, Ex-Yugoslav, Ex-Soviet, or the Greek-Cypriot pair), the average points awarded is 5.26. When the recipient is outside the bloc, the average is 2.31 - a 2.27x ratio. The Greek-Cypriot pair is by far the most extreme: the average vote between Greece and Cyprus is 10.98 points, almost five times their average vote to anyone outside their pair (2.25). The Ex-Yugoslav bloc averages 7.40 in-bloc vs 1.99 out-of-bloc; the Nordic bloc 4.88 vs 2.19; the Ex-Soviet bloc 4.64 vs 1.79.

calculation.output:
in-bloc mean points: 5.255
out-of-bloc mean points: 2.311
ratio in/out: 2.27
Greek-Cypriot 10.984 / 2.248
Ex-Yugoslav   7.396 / 1.987
Nordic        4.879 / 2.193
Ex-Soviet     4.638 / 1.791

data_table.description: In-bloc vs out-of-bloc average points awarded per pair, by bloc.

ana_05.label: The 2009 jury reform barely moved the bloc-vote needle
ana_05.content: When the EBU re-introduced 50/50 jury+televote scoring in 2009, the explicit goal was to dilute Eastern-bloc and other regional alliances. The data show the reform shaved bloc bias only modestly. Pre-2009, in-bloc votes averaged 5.61 points and out-of-bloc 2.54 (ratio 2.21). Post-2009, in-bloc averaged 5.03 and out-of-bloc 2.10 (ratio 2.40). The absolute gap shrank by about 0.5 points but the in/out-bloc ratio actually grew slightly. Bloc voting persists in roughly the same proportions; the reform reshuffled which entries win, not how regions vote for each other.

calculation.output:
post-2009 reform: same_bloc=False -> 2.097, same_bloc=True -> 5.027
pre-2009 reform:  same_bloc=False -> 2.541, same_bloc=True -> 5.605

data_table.description: Mean points awarded per country-to-country vote by era and bloc relationship.

ana_06.label: Ukraine 2022: a 240-point televote spread between jury and public
ana_06.content: Kalush Orchestra's 'Stefania' won Eurovision 2022 with 631 total points and a final ranking of 1st. Inside that total, the dataset shows a 192-to-432 split: 192 points from juries (4th by jury behind the United Kingdom's 282, Sweden's 253, and Spain's 227) and 432 from the televote (1st by a wide margin - over Moldova's 227 and Serbia's 225). The televote tally includes 28 maximum 12-point allocations from 39 voting countries - over 70% of all televoting nations gave Ukraine top marks. The jury tally included only 5 of 39 maximum scores. This is the cleanest modern example of a viewer-driven empathy vote overriding a jury preference.

calculation.output:
Ukraine 2022 jury sum: 192 (39 voters), mean 4.92
Ukraine 2022 televote sum: 432 (39 voters), mean 11.08
Televote 12-point count: 28; jury 12-point count: 5

data_table.description: Top countries by jury and televote totals in Eurovision 2022 final.

notable_instance.name: Kalush Orchestra - Stefania (2022)
notable_instance.value: 192 jury points vs 432 televote points; 28 of 39 televote 12s
notable_instance.why: The defining 2022 moment: the televote-driven win that the jury reform could not contain.

ana_07.label: Sweden is the all-time 12-point favorite
ana_07.content: Across all final-round votes since 1975, Sweden has been awarded 12 points 110 times - more than any other country. Ukraine is second (83), the United Kingdom third (73), Italy fourth (72), Greece fifth (70). Russia (69), Ireland (66), France (61), Germany (57), Norway (56) round out the top 10. The Swedish lead reflects both consistent quality (60 grand-final appearances, average rank 8.4) and Nordic/diaspora goodwill that pre-dates the pure-televote era.

calculation.output: Sweden 110, Ukraine 83, United Kingdom 73, Italy 72, Greece 70, Russia 69, Ireland 66, France 61, Germany 57, Norway 56, Denmark 52, Serbia 45, Spain 44, Cyprus 44, Israel 42

data_table.description: Top 15 countries by lifetime 12-point allocations received in finals since 1975.

ana_08.label: When jury and public completely disagreed
ana_08.content: Since the EBU started publishing split jury/televote scores in 2016, several entries finished at opposite ends of the two rankings. The largest gap belongs to Poland's 2016 entry 'Color Of Your Life' by Michał Szpak - 25th by jury but 3rd by public, a 22-place spread. Australia 2017 went the other way (4th jury, 25th tele), as did Sweden 2018 (2nd jury, 23rd tele). Moldova's 2022 'Trenuletul' was 20th by jury but 2nd by televote. These splits are exactly what the 50/50 reform was designed to combine without privileging either taste.

calculation.output:
2016 Poland: jury rank 25, tele rank 3, diff 22
2017 Australia: jury 4, tele 25, diff 21
2018 Sweden: jury 2, tele 23, diff 21
2022 Moldova: jury 20, tele 2, diff 18
2019 Norway: jury 18, tele 1, diff 17
2021 Bulgaria: jury 6, tele 18, diff 12

data_table.description: Annual maximum jury-vs-televote rank divergence since the 2016 split-score era.

ana_09.label: Norway has the most last-place finishes
ana_09.content: Across grand finals (and pre-2004 finals), Norway has finished bottom 11 times - more than any other country. Germany and Belgium have 10 each; Finland 9; Austria 7; Switzerland and the Netherlands 6 each; Spain, the United Kingdom and Luxembourg 5 each. Norway's last-place count reflects a long-but-uneven history: 57 grand-final appearances and 3 wins (1985 'La Det Swinge', 1995 'Nocturne', 2009 'Fairytale').

calculation.output: Norway 11, Germany 10, Belgium 10, Finland 9, Austria 7, Switzerland 6, Netherlands 6, Spain 5, United Kingdom 5, Luxembourg 5, Portugal 4, France 3, Malta 3, Italy 3, Turkey 3

data_table.description: Countries with the most last-place finishes in finals/grand-finals.

ana_10.label: Salvador Sobral's 2017 Portugal: highest single-final point total
ana_10.content: The largest point total ever recorded in a single grand final in this dataset is Salvador Sobral's 758 points for Portugal in 2017 - 'Amar Pelos Dois', a sparse jazz ballad. Ukraine 2022 (631) is second. Bulgaria 2017 (615, 2nd-place that year) and Ukraine 2016 (534) follow. Five of the top 10 single-final totals are post-2016, reflecting both the new ranked-list scoring system (introduced in 2016, which mathematically allows much larger totals) and the swelling field of 26 finalists.

calculation.output: Portugal 2017 Sobral 758, Ukraine 2022 Kalush 631, Bulgaria 2017 Kostov 615, Ukraine 2016 Jamala 534, Israel 2018 Netta 529, Italy 2021 Maneskin 524, Australia 2016 Dami Im 511, France 2021 Pravi 499, Netherlands 2019 Laurence 498

data_table.description: Top 10 highest point totals in any single Eurovision final.

ana_11.label: Winners by region across decades shows the Eastern shift in the 2000s
ana_11.content: Of all 69 winning entries from 1956-2022, 41 went to Western European countries, 13 to Nordic, 9 to Eastern Europe, and 6 to Mediterranean (Greece, Cyprus, Turkey, Israel). The era-shift is dramatic. The 1950s produced four winners, all Western. The 1960s 12 of 13 Western. Eastern Europe did not win once until Yugoslavia in 1989. From 2000-2009, however, Eastern Europe produced 5 of 10 winners (Estonia 2001, Latvia 2002, Ukraine 2004, Serbia 2007, Russia 2008) and Western Europe produced exactly zero - the only decade in which the Western bloc was shut out.

ana_12.label: Field expansion: the 2003-2004 jump and the move to semi-finals
ana_12.content: The number of competing countries per year tripled across the dataset's life. Eurovision 1956 had 7 entries; through the late 1980s it hovered between 18 and 22; by 2003 it reached 26. The 2004 contest's introduction of semi-finals (and the 2008 split into two semis) opened the door wider: 36 entries that year, then steadily 39-43 from 2008 onward. The 2022 contest had 40 unique countries fielding entries across all rounds.

data_table.description: Unique countries entering Eurovision per year.

ana_13.label: Ireland's three-in-a-row and the Logan effect
ana_13.content: Ireland is the only country to win Eurovision in three consecutive years: 1992 (Linda Martin, 'Why Me'), 1993 (Niamh Kavanagh, 'In Your Eyes'), and 1994 (Paul Harrington and Charlie McGettigan, 'Rock 'n' Roll Kids'). They added a fourth win in 1996 (Eimear Quinn, 'The Voice'), making four wins in five years. Johnny Logan won in 1980 and 1987, and is the only person to win as a performer twice. With Dana's 1970 win and these six others, Ireland had 7 Eurovision wins by 1996 - the record that stood unmatched until Sweden equalled it in 2023.

calculation.output:
1970 Dana - All Kinds Of Everything (32 pts)
1980 Johnny Logan - What's Another Year (143)
1987 Johnny Logan - Hold Me Now (172)
1992 Linda Martin - Why Me (155)
1993 Niamh Kavanagh - In Your Eyes (187)
1994 Paul Harrington and Charlie McGettigan - Rock 'n' Roll Kids (226)
1996 Eimear Quinn - The Voice (162)

ana_14.label: Most-favored sending pairs by total points (chord-diagram input)
ana_14.content: The single largest historical point flow between two countries is Cyprus to Greece - 394 points across all final voting since 1975. Denmark to Sweden is second with 366; Norway to Sweden 360; Greece to Cyprus 331. The top 10 sending pairs by sum points are dominated by Nordic-internal flows (Denmark-Sweden, Norway-Sweden, Finland-Sweden, Iceland-Sweden, Sweden-Norway), the Greek-Cypriot bilateral, the Iberian Portugal-Spain pair, and the Anglo-Irish exchange. This is the input shape Designer can render as a chord or arc diagram showing 'who votes for whom most'.

ana_15.label: Greece <-> Cyprus 12-point exchange across years
ana_15.content: Looking only at years where both Greece and Cyprus competed in the final and were eligible to vote for each other, the data show 13 of 24 years with both giving 12 points - 54% mutual maximum. The streak peaked from 1997 to 2005, when both countries gave each other 12 in 8 consecutive contests. The pattern wobbled in the late 2000s (Cyprus didn't qualify some years) but resumed: 2010, 2012, 2017, 2019, 2021 all featured the mutual 12. The most striking single-year break was 2015, when both gave their 12 to Italy (Il Volo's 'Grande Amore') instead of each other.

calculation.output:
1997-1998-2002-2003-2004-2005-2010-2012-2017-2019-2021: both 12s (and 1987, 1994)
Years both competed and traded points: 24
Years both gave each other 12: 13

data_table.description: Cyprus->Greece and Greece->Cyprus point totals per year (both competed).

ana_16.label: Iconic three: ABBA 1974, Lordi 2006, Conchita 2014
ana_16.content: Three of the contest's culturally largest wins are anchored in the data. ABBA's 1974 'Waterloo' for Sweden won with 24 points (under the older voting cap) and was voted Eurovision's all-time best song at the 2005 50th-anniversary special. Lordi's 'Hard Rock Hallelujah' won 2006 for Finland with 292 points - a record at the time and Finland's only Eurovision win. Austria's Conchita Wurst won 2014 with 'Rise Like a Phoenix' on 290 points; the win was widely framed as a statement on LGBTQ+ visibility in Europe. All three winners can be embedded directly via the Eurovision Song Contest's official YouTube channel.

calculation.output:
1974 Sweden ABBA Waterloo 24 pts (rank 1)
2006 Finland Lordi Hard Rock Hallelujah 292 (1)
2014 Austria Conchita Wurst Rise Like a Phoenix 290 (1)

data_table.description: Three iconic Eurovision wins anchoring the cultural-history thread.

caveats.content: Country names in the dataset evolved with geopolitics (Yugoslavia, Serbia & Montenegro, F.Y.R. Macedonia / North Macedonia). The bloc analysis treats each name as recorded; cross-name aggregation would shift exact totals slightly but not the magnitudes.

The eurovision-votes.csv file ends in 2019 (despite 2022 entries appearing); the 2022 votes are present but the dataset's grand-final pairwise totals for 2022 sum to 624 for Ukraine (192 jury + 432 televote) where the canonical official total in eurovision.csv is 631. We use the 631 official total in headline numbers and the 192/432 split for the jury-vs-televote breakdown.
Eurovision 2020 was cancelled due to COVID; 41 countries' intended entries appear in the dataset with NaN scores. We exclude 2020 from rank-based analyses.
Pre-2009 'final' rows and 2004+ 'grand-final' rows are treated as the same competition tier.
